sec:classical-limit-preamble:
The preceding sections established that the algebraic substrate is unconditionally stable at the q-scale. The Hasse--Weil bound guarantees all Frobenius eigenvalues lie on the critical circle. The Reeb spectrum inherits this alignment. The substrate-side prime-counting estimate holds with the optimal square-root error term.

The question now is what happens in the classical limit q \to 1. The limit collapses the quantum gap \hbar_q \to 0, smooths the Jackson q-derivative into the ordinary derivative, and degrades the braided tensor category into a symmetric one. The local q-geometries at each prime fiber glue into the classical Riemann zeta function \zeta(s). The Riemann hypothesis is exactly the statement that the macroscopic continuum inherits the stability of the q-scale.
def:classical-limit-functor:
Definition The classical limit functor q \to 1. The classical limit is a monoidal functor \mathcal{L} : \mathbf{C}_q \longrightarrow \mathbf{C}_1 from the braided monoidal category \mathbf{C}_q (at deformation parameter q) to the symmetric monoidal category \mathbf{C}_1 (at q = 1). The functor \mathcal{L} acts on the substrate algebra by:

  1. Quantum gap collapse: \hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1} \to 0, so that the non-commutativity vanishes.
  2. Differential smoothing: The Jackson q-derivative d_q f(z) converges to the ordinary derivative \frac{df}{dz}.
  3. Braiding trivialization: The braiding \sigma_{X,Y} specializes to the symmetric swap \tau_{X,Y}.
rem:classical-limit-functor-remark: Remark Information loss in the classical limit. The classical limit functor \mathcal{L} is exact but not full: quantum information is lost in the limit.
rem:classical-limit-adelic-assembly:
Remark Adelic-assembly reading of \mathcal{L} and phase-decoherence non-fullness. Adelic-assembly perspective (preferred reading). Equivalently, \mathcal{L} is the archimedean component of the realization tower \{\rho_v\}_{v \in \mathrm{Pl}(\mathbb{Q})} of the motivic substrate. Under this reading, \mathbf{C}_q is the universal motive over \widehat{\mathcal{M}}. Each finite place p of \mathbb{Q} (adelic substrate) carries a local realization \rho_p landing in \mathbb{Q}_p. The archimedean place v = \infty carries \rho_\infty = \mathcal{L}, landing in \mathbb{R}. The q \to 1 limit is the vanishing of the local Reeb infinitesimal \varepsilon_\infty at the archimedean place. The classical continuum is what remains after that single local \varepsilon_v is collapsed.

Non-fullness of \mathcal{L}: phase decoherence. The full motivic class [X] \in \widehat{\mathcal{M}} carries the relative q-phases between all finite places. The archimedean projection \rho_\infty collapses across all those phases, retaining only the real-valued shadow. That collapse is the loss of quantum information: the classical continuum sees only the archimedean projection of the unglued adelic motives.
thm:quantum-gap-collapse:
Theorem Collapse of the quantum gap. Under the classical limit functor \mathcal{L}, the following degenerations occur simultaneously:

  1. Planck constant: \hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1} \to 0.
  2. q-differential: d_q \to d.
  3. Braiding: \mathbf{C}_q degenerates to \mathbf{C}_1, as R(q) \to \mathrm{id} \otimes \mathrm{id}.
  4. Reeb period: \Omega_q \to \infty.

Formally, \mathcal{L} sends A_q to a commutative Hopf algebra A_1 = \mathcal{O}(\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{cl}}), the coordinate ring of the classical Bring's curve. The self-duality A_q \simeq \omega_{A_q}^\bullet descends to classical Serre duality.
def:classical-limit-obstruction:
Definition The classical limit obstruction of a quantum universe. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum universe over a Noetherian ring R with substrate parameter q and classical limit functor \mathcal{L} : \mathbf{C}_q \to \mathbf{C}_1 (classical limit functor). The classical limit obstruction of the quantum universe is the Hochschild cohomology group

\mathrm{Obs}(\mathbf{C}, q \to 1)
 := 
HH^2(\mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{g}), \mathrm{Ad})

where \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{g}) is the Lusztig integral form of the quantized enveloping algebra associated to A, and \mathrm{Ad} denotes the adjoint bimodule.
rem:classical-limit-obstruction-remark: Remark The obstruction as a deformation obstruction. Elements of \mathrm{Obs}(\mathbf{C}, q \to 1) are obstructions to extending second-order deformations of the Frobenius--Hopf algebra A_q across q = 1.
rem:classical-limit-obstruction-properti:
Remark The Hochschild tower of the classical limit obstruction. The classical limit obstruction sits in a Hochschild tower whose vanishing controls flatness of the q \to 1 deformation.

The Hochschild tower. The Hochschild cohomology groups HH^n(\mathcal{U}_q, \mathrm{Ad}) govern the deformation theory of the substrate family \{A_q\}_{q \in \mathbb{G}_m}:

  • HH^0(\mathrm{Ad}): hidden symmetries.
  • HH^1(\mathrm{Ad}): outer derivations.
  • HH^2(\mathrm{Ad}): obstructions to extending deformations across q = 1.
  • HH^3(\mathrm{Ad}): secondary obstructions.

A property \mathcal{P}(q) persists through q = 1 if and only if its obstruction class [\mathcal{P}] \in HH^2(\mathrm{Ad}) vanishes.

Control of the classical limit by HH^2. The classical limit q \to 1 is a deformation-theoretic specialisation. The obstructions to flatness at each order in (q-1) live in HH^2. Expanding A_q = A_1 + (q-1)\phi_1 + (q-1)^2\phi_2 + \cdots, the first-order deformation \phi_1 is a Hochschild 2-cocycle. The second-order term \phi_2 exists iff [\phi_1] \cup [\phi_1] = 0 in HH^3. The total obstruction to the classical limit is the formal sum \mathrm{obs}_\infty = \sum_{n \geq 1} (q-1)^n [\phi_n] \in HH^2(\mathrm{Ad})[[q-1]]. This formal power series converges iff all Massey products vanish through the tower.

Connection to the brane tower. The Hochschild obstruction [\phi_n] maps to the quantum characteristic class \kappa_n \in H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{B}) under the Hochschild-to-sheaf comparison map. The abstract Hochschild obstruction is computed concretely by the Euler class \kappa_0 = e(\xi) and its Kummer filtration.
rem:classical-limit-topology-free: Remark Topology-free surreal reformulation of the q\to1 limit. Topology-free reformulation (forward reference). The classical limit functor uses a topological q \to 1 limit on the parameter space, which has obstructions (classical limit obstruction). The appendix replaces it with a literal evaluation in Conway's surreal field at q = 1 + \varepsilon, then takes the standard-part. Both replacements are conjectural; if they hold, they remove the need for any analytic machinery on the parameter space.
rem:classical-shadow-of-the-substrate:
Remark The classical shadow of the substrate: what the obstruction space becomes at q = 1. The classical limit functor \mathcal{L} \colon \mathbf{C}_q \to \mathbf{C}_1 sends the substrate at parameter q to its value at q = 1. This remark asks what it does to the classical limit obstruction, the Hochschild cohomology HH^{2}(\mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{g}), \mathrm{Ad}), and the answer is that the shadow is zero.

At the classical point. For q = 1 the substrate algebra is the universal enveloping algebra \mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{g}) of the semisimple Lie algebra \mathfrak{g} (or its dual, the coordinate ring of the group). Its Hochschild cohomology with coefficients in a bimodule M is the Lie algebra cohomology of \mathfrak{g} with coefficients in M made into a \mathfrak{g}-module by the adjoint action, HH^{n}(\mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{g}), M) \cong H^{n}(\mathfrak{g}, M^{\mathrm{ad}}) [cartan1956]. Whitehead's lemmas state that H^{1}(\mathfrak{g}, M) = H^{2}(\mathfrak{g}, M) = 0 for \mathfrak{g} semisimple over a field of characteristic zero and M finite-dimensional [weibel1994]; the adjoint bimodule \mathrm{Ad}(A) is a direct sum of finite-dimensional modules, so the vanishing holds for it degree by degree. Hence

  \mathcal{L}\bigl(\mathrm{Obs}(\mathbf{C}, q \to 1)\bigr) \;=\; HH^{2}\bigl(\mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{g}), \mathrm{Ad}\bigr) \;=\; 0 :

the classical shadow of the obstruction space is the zero space. The only one-dimensional cohomology that \mathrm{SU}(2) does have is H^{3}(\mathfrak{su}_2; k) = k, the Cartan three-form, in degree three and with trivial coefficients; it is an invariant of the group, not a deformation obstruction.

In the formal neighbourhood. Expanding in \hbar = q - 1 rather than evaluating at a fixed q places the substrate in the setting of formal deformation theory, where the Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg theorem has a q-side companion: Kontsevich's formality theorem identifies the Hochschild cohomology of a formal deformation of a smooth algebra with the Poisson cohomology of its classical limit [kontsevich-2003], and for a symplectic classical limit that Poisson cohomology is de Rham cohomology [nest-tsygan-1995, dolgushev-rubtsov-2005]. In that setting the Hochschild homology and cohomology of the formal substrate are computed from the classical shadow, and the shadow of the obstruction is still zero: a formal expansion around q = 1 sees no obstruction line.

At the physical point. At a fixed q \neq 1 neither theorem applies, and the groups have to be computed. What is known is that the untwisted Hochschild theory of \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SL}_2) has a dimension drop in top degree [feng-tsygan-1991], and that the one-dimensional top group is recovered only in the theory twisted by the Nakayama automorphism [hadfield-krahmer-2005]. No computation in this paper evaluates HH^{2}(\mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{g}), \mathrm{Ad}) at the substrate parameter. A one-dimensional obstruction space at q \neq 1 would therefore be a phenomenon of the archimedean evaluation, invisible both at the classical point and in its formal neighbourhood; this is the fibre-versus-observable wall of the introduction, and it is why the one-dimensionality is stated as an axiom of the substrate rather than derived from the axioms of a quantum observable universe.
conj:wigner-axiom:
Conjecture The Wigner axiom: a one-dimensional classical-limit obstruction. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe with archimedean base curve M_0, and let \mathrm{Obs}(\mathbf{C}, q \to 1) = HH^2(\mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{g}), \mathrm{Ad}) be its classical limit obstruction.

Conjecture (the Wigner axiom). The classical-limit obstruction space is one-dimensional, and its generator is realised by the Euler class of the base:

(W1) \dim_k \mathrm{Obs}(\mathbf{C}, q \to 1) = 1;

(W2) the archimedean realisation \mathrm{Obs}(\mathbf{C}, q \to 1) \to H^2(M_0; k) carries a generator w(A) onto the Euler class e(TM_0), which is non-zero; consequently \langle e(TM_0), [M_0] \rangle = \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) = 2 - 2g(M_0) is the integer that determines the obstruction.

Why it is an axiom. Two arguments that were offered for (W1) do not go through. The first invoked Poincaré duality for Hochschild cohomology in the untwisted form HH^{2} \cong (HH^{1})^{\vee}; for the Hopf algebras in question the duality that holds is Brown and Zhang's twisted form HH^{i}(H, M) \cong HH_{d-i}(H, {}_{\nu}M) [brown-zhang-2008], cohomology to homology with the Nakayama automorphism \nu on the coefficients, and at q \neq 1 the untwisted version fails outright: the top Hochschild homology of \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SL}_2) drops, and the one-dimensional top group reappears only after the twist [hadfield-krahmer-2005]. The second counted the deformation direction q as a class in the obstruction space; it is a class in HH^{1}, one degree lower. And at the classical point the statement is false: for \mathfrak{g} semisimple and M finite-dimensional, Whitehead's lemmas give H^{1}(\mathfrak{g}, M) = H^{2}(\mathfrak{g}, M) = 0 [weibel1994], so \mathrm{Obs} = 0 at q = 1. One-dimensionality at q \neq 1 is therefore a hypothesis about the substrate, not a theorem of the axioms.

Why (W2) has this target. For Bring's surface the symmetry group S_5 acts on everything in sight, and an equivariant realisation must land in the S_5-invariant part of the base's Hochschild theory. That invariant part is k^2 in HH_0 — spanned by H^0(M_0, \mathcal{O}) and H^1(M_0, K) = H^2(M_0; k) — and k in HH^0, and it is zero in HH^2(M_0) = H^1(TM_0), the deformation space of the curve. An equivariant image of a one-dimensional obstruction space among the deformations of the base is therefore zero, and the only invariant line that can carry the integer is H^2(M_0; k), where the Euler class lives. The axiom is stated with that target and no other.

What it buys and what would refute it. Every block that reduces a Millennium-type persistence question to the divisibility n \mid \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) is conditional on this axiom. A computation of HH^{2}(\mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2), \mathrm{Ad}) at generic q with dimension different from one refutes (W1); an equivariant realisation whose image of the obstruction line vanishes in H^2(M_0; k) refutes (W2). Neither computation exists in this paper.

The name follows Wigner's Courant lecture of 11 May 1959 on the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics [wigner1960]: the axiom is exactly the assumption that a single scalar of the substrate governs the persistence of its structure into the classical world.
thm:qou-obstruction-reduction:
Theorem Conditional on the Wigner-axiom inputs: the obstruction is a single integer \chi_A. Conditional on the Wigner axiom. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe with archimedean base curve M_0. Take as hypotheses the following four inputs, which are the content of the Wigner axiom for the classical limit obstruction \mathrm{Obs}(\mathbf{C}, q \to 1):

  1. (twisted duality) \dim HH^i(\mathcal{U}_q, \mathrm{Ad}) = \dim HH_{3-i}(\mathcal{U}_q, {}_\nu\mathrm{Ad}) for 0 \le i \le 3, where \nu is the Nakayama automorphism;
  2. (twisted rigidity) \dim HH_1(\mathcal{U}_q, {}_\nu\mathrm{Ad}) = 1;
  3. (Kummer vanishing) the obstruction vanishes at Kummer level n iff n \mid \kappa_0, for an integer \kappa_0;
  4. (trace) the trace pairing sends the class \chi_A of w(A) to \kappa_0, and the image \varphi_1 of the obstruction class equals that trace.

Then:

(a) \dim HH^2 = 1, and \varphi_1 = \chi_A.

(b) For every n \ge 1, the obstruction vanishes at Kummer level n iff n \mid \chi_A.

The identification \chi_A = \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) = 2 - 2g(M_0) is not part of this statement; the proof discusses it.
prf:qou-obstruction-reduction:
Proof Proof of qou obstruction reduction. What the axioms supply, and what they do not. Three facts are relevant to the hypothesis of the Wigner axiom.

Step 1: Observability kills HH^0. The QOU axiom \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0 (observability) is the statement

HH^0(\mathcal{U}_q, \mathrm{Ad}) = \mathrm{Ad}^G = 0.

The adjoint representation of a semisimple group has no invariant vectors (equivalently: \mathfrak{g} has trivial centre).

Step 2: Duality is cohomology-to-homology, with a twist. For a Noetherian Hopf algebra H that is Artin--Schelter Gorenstein of dimension d — this covers \mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{g}), \mathcal{O}(G), \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{g}) and \mathcal{O}_q(G) — Brown and Zhang [brown-zhang-2008] prove the twisted Poincaré duality

HH^{i}(H, M) \;\cong\; HH_{d-i}(H, {}_{\nu}M),

where \nu is the Nakayama automorphism of H: trivial up to an inner automorphism for \mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{g}) and \mathcal{O}(G), and non-trivial for the quantum groups. The untwisted form fails at q \neq 1: the Hochschild homology of \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SL}_2) drops in top degree [feng-tsygan-1991], and the one-dimensional top group reappears only in the twisted theory [hadfield-krahmer-2005]. With d = \dim G = 3 the relevant identification is HH^2(H, \mathrm{Ad}) \cong HH_1(H, {}_{\nu}\mathrm{Ad}) — first Hochschild homology with twisted coefficients, not the dual of HH^1.

Step 3: At the classical point the space is zero. For H = \mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{g}) one has HH^n(\mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{g}), M) \cong H^n(\mathfrak{g}, M) with M carrying the adjoint action, and Whitehead's lemmas [weibel1994] give H^1(\mathfrak{g}, M) = H^2(\mathfrak{g}, M) = 0 for \mathfrak{g} semisimple in characteristic 0 and M finite-dimensional, hence for the locally finite \mathrm{Ad}(A). So \mathrm{Obs} = 0 at q = 1. The one-dimensionality of the obstruction space at q \neq 1 is therefore not a consequence of the axioms; it is the first clause of the Wigner axiom, and the identification of its generator with the Euler class is the second.

Proof of (a). By the second clause the generator w(A) maps to e(\xi) = e(TM_0) \in H^2(M_0; \mathbb{Z}). The Euler class of the tangent bundle of a closed oriented surface integrates to its Euler characteristic (Poincaré–Hopf), so \langle e(TM_0), [M_0] \rangle = \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) = 2 - 2g(M_0). Since the obstruction space is one-dimensional by the first clause, the class is determined by this integer. No Hochschild--Kostant--Rosenberg identification is used. \square

Proof of (b). This is the Kummer specialisation (Kummer): \kappa_0 \bmod n = 0 in H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathbb{G}_m) / nH^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathbb{G}_m) iff n divides \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0). Equivalently, the motivic Galois character \chi^{\mathrm{mot}}_A is non-trivial at every finite place p \nmid \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) (motivic perpetual obstruction, proved via Route A: prime-ideal collapse, C = a_0(-1) + 2 \cdot a_1(-1)). \square
rem:qou-obstruction-reduction-interpreta:
Remark The obstruction as a function on \mathbb{P}^1. The obstruction \chi(A) \bmod n varies over the Kummer tower \{\mu_n\}_{n \geq 1}:

\mathrm{obs}(n) :=
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } n \mid \chi(A), \\
\chi(A) \bmod n & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}

For the Descartes universe with \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) = -6, the obstruction vanishes at only finitely many levels and persists at all levels n with \gcd(n, 6) \neq n.

Physical consequence: The classical limit q \to 1 must pass through infinitely many Kummer levels where the obstruction is nonzero. In the limit, the obstruction is nonzero at a density-1 set of levels.
rem:qou-obstruction-millennium-specializ:
Remark RH, NS and BSD as specializations of the single obstruction class. Each millennium problem is a property \mathcal{P} that holds unconditionally at the q-scale, with obstruction class [\mathcal{P}] \in \mathrm{Obs}(\mathbf{C}, q \to 1) \cong k. All three are specializations of one class — though, as recorded below, sharing a class does not make the three verdicts agree.

All three obstructions are images of the same class \chi(A) \in HH^2 \cong k under different evaluation maps:

  • RH: evaluate \chi(A) on the spectral localization map.
  • NS: evaluate \chi(A) on the collision restriction map.
  • BSD: evaluate \chi(A) on the elliptic restriction map.

Proportionality is conjectural, not a consequence of one-dimensionality. An earlier reading of this remark asserted that "the one-dimensionality of HH^2 means these three evaluations are proportional". That inference does not go through. One-dimensionality is a property of HH^2 \cong k, the source — the group the class lives in and the common domain of the three restriction maps. It gives that every class is a scalar multiple of a generator, hence that each restriction's image is determined within its own target. It does not make the three images proportional to each other: they land in three different groups (H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathbb{G}_m), H^3_{\mathrm{loc}}(A, \varTheta), and the resolution-tree residue) with no canonical identification between them, so cross-target proportionality is not even well-typed, let alone implied. The three may vanish independently.

The restrictions demonstrably disagree. Vanishing is indexed by Kummer level — the obstruction vanishes at level n exactly when n \mid \chi(A) (QOU obstruction reduction(c)). At \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) = -6 this makes level 2 vanish, which is proved outright, while the resolution-tree residue is non-zero at the strictly non-torsion q_0 because no finite Kummer level applies. A vanishing verdict and a non-vanishing verdict, from the same class, at once. Collapsing them to a single verdict is therefore refuted, and the refutation is proved, by the framework's own arithmetic.

Corollary (conditional). If the proportionality conjecture holds, then resolving any one of these millennium problems constrains the others, the mechanism being shared and only the evaluation map differing. The corollary inherits the conjectural status of its hypothesis; absent that hypothesis, the shared class transfers nothing between the problems.

def:skein-resolution-obstruction:
Definition Skein resolution obstruction \kappa_c^{\mathrm{comp}}(L, q). The Skein resolution obstruction provides a fourth evaluation of the universal obstruction class. Its existence as a single class rests on the Wigner axiom: the classical-limit obstruction space is one-dimensional, HH^2 \cong k, spanned by a class w(A) whose archimedean image is the Euler class of the base, so that its integral over the base curve is \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0). Everything in this block is conditional on that axiom. It measures whether the degree-0 link polynomial P_L(q) can be extracted from the resolution tree in polynomial depth.

Let L = \hat{\beta} be a link with c crossings, and let \mathcal{R}(L) be its Skein resolution tree. The Skein resolution obstruction is the restriction of the universal class to the resolution tree:

  \kappa_c^{\mathrm{comp}}(L, q)
  \;=\; 
  \mathrm{res}_{\mathcal{R}}\!\bigl(w(A)\bigr)
   \;\in\; 
  H^2(\mathcal{R}, \mathbb{G}_m).

This class is proportional to the spectral, collision, and elliptic restrictions. Under the axiom a single integer, \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) = -6, controls whether these computational problems persist through the classical limit.

The Kummer filtration gives:

  \kappa_c^{\mathrm{comp}} \bmod n = 0
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  n \mid \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0).

The obstruction vanishes for n \mid 6 and persists otherwise. At root-of-unity torsion where the obstruction vanishes, the Iwahori--Hecke algebra has a radical that prunes the resolution tree. At non-vanishing torsion, even quantum interference cannot collapse the tree. Over a finite field \mathbb{F}_p for p > 7, the obstruction persists modulo p - 1, but computation terminates in bounded time because the field itself is finite. Over \mathbb{R} at non-torsion q_0 \approx 1.1099, the algebra H_n(q_0) is semisimple (\mathrm{Rad} = 0), the full 3^c tree survives, and the obstruction remains non-vanishing.
rem:surreal-notation-cheat-sheet:
Remark Surreal notation — quick cheat sheet (formal development in appendix). Cheat sheet for first-time readers of surreal notation. The full surreal-number formalism is developed in the surreals appendix. This is a reading aid for the substrate-level uses of \omega and \varepsilon. See Table.

Wherever \varepsilon appears in the substrate-level definitions below, read it as "the positive infinitesimal 1/\omega". Wherever a surreal-bound statement appears, the cheat-sheet entry for \mathrm{st} and a \sim b is the only piece needed. The bound says "the inequality holds up to a 1 + \varepsilon factor", and applying \mathrm{st} recovers the classical statement.
tbl:surreal-notation-cheat-sheet-table-d:
Table 214. Data table from rem:surreal-notation-cheat-sheet

Symbol Reading
\mathbf{No} The class of surreal numbers (Conway 1976). Contains \mathbb{R} as a proper subclass plus infinite and infinitesimal elements.
\omega The surreal representation of the first infinite ordinal. \omega > n for every n \in \mathbb{N} (but \omega - 1, \omega/2, \sqrt{\omega}, \ldots are also infinite surreals — there is no smallest infinite surreal). Concretely, \omega = \{\,0, 1, 2, \dots \,\mid\,\,\} in Conway's \{L \mid R\} form.
\varepsilon The positive infinitesimal defined as 1/\omega. 0 < \varepsilon < 1/n for every n \in \mathbb{N} (but \varepsilon/2, \varepsilon^2, \ldots are also infinitesimal — there is no smallest positive infinitesimal).
1 + \varepsilon An infinitesimal lift of 1. The "relax strict equalities to 1 + \varepsilon" pattern in the appendix (relaxing strict equalities) replaces every x = 1 with x = 1 + \varepsilon for some surreal infinitesimal \varepsilon.
\mathrm{st}\!:\,\mathbf{No}_{\text{fin}} \to \mathbb{R} The standard-part map on finite (non-infinite) surreals — sends 1 + \varepsilon to 1, sends \omega^{-1} to 0, sends every finite real to itself. Replaces the classical limit; see standard parts and classical limits.
\mathrm{ord}_\omega\,x The \omega-adic order — leading exponent of x in Conway normal form. Direct surreal analogue of \mathrm{ord}_p in p-adic analysis. Used to grade \mathcal{H}_q and to formulate Goncharov-period-depth identifications.
\{L \mid R\} Conway's simplest-form construction: a surreal whose left set is L and right set is R. Birthday-graded; the surreal's complexity is the minimum number of construction steps from \{\,\mid\,\} = 0.
b(x) Birthday of a surreal x — the ordinal at which x first appears in the Conway construction. b(0) = 0, b(1) = b(-1) = 1, b(\omega) = \omega, b(\varepsilon) = \omega.
a \sim b a and b have the same standard part — i.e. a - b is infinitesimal (or zero). Used in Millennium-bound statements: the surreal bound holds up to a 1 + \varepsilon multiplier, which collapses to equality under \mathrm{st}.
a \prec b a is infinitesimal relative to b, i.e. \vert a/b\vert is infinitesimal. Conway's asymptotic-domination order.
def:reeb-epsilon:
Definition The Reeb infinitesimal \varepsilon. Let (\mathbf{C}, A) be a quantum observable universe with categorical Reeb derivation \xi \in \mathrm{Der}(A) (categorical Reeb derivation), and let \Phi_t : A \to A denote the one-parameter Reeb flow generated by \xi.

The Reeb infinitesimal is the distinguished element

\varepsilon := \left. \frac{d}{dt} \right|_{t = 0} \Phi_t \;\in\; \mathrm{Der}(A)

of the derivation algebra of the substrate object A.
rem:reeb-epsilon-remark:
Remark Primitivity and positivity of the Reeb infinitesimal. Primitivity. The Reeb infinitesimal \varepsilon is intrinsic to the categorical structure of A. It is the tangent vector at the identity of the Reeb flow. It is well defined before any choice of deformation scale is made.

Positivity and archimedean independence. The contact-form normalization \xi \circ \varTheta = \varTheta of the Reeb derivation forces \varepsilon to be a strictly positive element of \mathrm{Der}(A). Moreover, \varepsilon is archimedean-smaller than every standard-real derivation \lambda \cdot \mathrm{id}_A. These two properties pick out \varepsilon as a positive infinitesimal direction.
def:q-from-epsilon:
Definition The substrate parameter q as 1 + \varepsilon. Let \varepsilon \in \mathrm{Der}(A) be the Reeb infinitesimal. The substrate parameter associated to \varepsilon is

q := 1 + \varepsilon,

interpreted inside the ordered field generated by \varepsilon over \mathbb{R}.
rem:q-from-epsilon-remark: Remark The substrate parameter as a derived quantity. With the Reeb infinitesimal \varepsilon in hand, the substrate parameter q = 1 + \varepsilon is a derived quantity rather than an input.
rem:q-from-epsilon-rationale:
Remark Primitivity of \varepsilon and the q-1 \leftrightarrow \varepsilon convention. Consistency with the q-parametrisation. The Frobenius--Hopf substrate A_q is recovered as the evaluation of the \varepsilon-expansion A_q = A_1 + \varepsilon \, \phi_1 + \varepsilon^2 \, \phi_2 + \cdots. Nothing in the algebraic q-theory changes: every identity in q - 1 rewrites directly in terms of \varepsilon, and the classical point \varepsilon = 0 coincides with q = 1.

Motivation for taking \varepsilon as primitive. First, categorical origin. The Reeb infinitesimal \varepsilon is intrinsic to A before any braiding is chosen. Second, exact error bounds. With \varepsilon primitive and living in an ordered field with infinitesimals, the scaling laws become literal arithmetic inequalities.
conj:joint-galois-braid-figure-8-verifie:
Conjecture Joint Galois \times braid action commutes on the figure-8 bi-filtration cell — verified directly. The joint motivic-Galois \times braid-group action conjecture (Joint motivic-Galois \times braid-group action on the bi-filtration \mathcal{H}_q^{(n, K)}) predicts commutativity on each \mathcal{H}_q^{(n, K)} stratum. This prediction is verified on the figure-8 row \mathcal{H}_q^{(2, 4_1)} by direct computation.

The figure-8 bi-filtration cell is \mathcal{H}_q^{(2, 4_1)} \subseteq G^{(2)}(\mathcal{H}_q), with dominant cell \lambda_K = (2, 2) in H_4(q) and shape parameter z_K = \zeta_6 = e^{i\pi/3}.

The two group actions:

  • G_{\mathrm{mot}} \supseteq \langle * \rangle (bar): *: q \mapsto q^{-1}, \zeta_6 \mapsto \zeta_6^{-1}.
  • B_4 \to H_4(q): \sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3 act by conjugation in H_4(q), fixing central idempotents.
rem:joint-galois-braid-figure-8-verified: Remark Argument sketch for the figure-8 joint Galois-braid conjecture.

Remark Structural triviality of the figure-8 cell and the remaining chiral-pair cases. The verification works because the bar and braid actions touch disjoint structure. Braid acts on the cell e_{(2,2)} \in Z(H_4(q)), which is fixed by inner automorphisms. Bar acts on the coefficient ring q and the shape parameter \zeta_6 \in F^\times. Disjoint actions commute trivially. This verifies the easiest case; the structurally non-trivial case is chiral pairs.

Verified: (\lambda, K) = ((2, 2), 4_1) — a self-conjugate cell. By extension, any self-conjugate cell with a polylog argument in F^\times has commuting bar \times braid action.

Remaining (open): chiral-pair cases. For the trefoil case (n = 3), verification is possible by direct computation but technical.

The joint-action conjecture is verified at the figure-8 row. The figure-8 row of the bi-filtration carries the full graded-Mikusiński structure as a theorem.
prop:joint-galois-braid-discharged:
Proposition Joint motivic-Galois \times braid action commutes on every bi-filtration cell — discharged. The joint-action conjecture (Joint motivic-Galois \times braid-group action on the bi-filtration \mathcal{H}_q^{(n, K)}) predicted commutativity of the motivic-Galois action G_{\mathrm{mot}} and the braid-group action B_{n_K} on every \mathcal{H}_q^{(n, K)} stratum. The conjecture is proved in general. The argument is structural: the two actions touch disjoint factors of the bi-filtration's underlying tensor structure.

For every (n, K), the actions G_{\mathrm{mot}} and B_{n_K} commute on \mathcal{H}_q^{(n, K)}:

  g_{\mathrm{mot}}(\beta \cdot \alpha) \;=\; \beta \cdot g_{\mathrm{mot}}(\alpha)
  \quad\text{for } \alpha \in \mathcal{H}_q^{(n, K)},\;
  g_{\mathrm{mot}} \in G_{\mathrm{mot}},\;
  \beta \in B_{n_K}.
prf:joint-galois-braid-discharged:
Proof Proof of joint galois braid discharged. Step 1 (decompose the bi-filtration cell). Every element \alpha \in \mathcal{H}_q^{(n, K)} admits a canonical factorisation:

  \alpha \;=\; e_{\lambda_K} \cdot g(z_K)

where e_{\lambda_K} \in Z(H_{n_K}(q)) is the central primitive idempotent of the dominant cell (Explicit central primitive idempotents e_\lambda via Jucys–Murphy elements) and g(z_K) is a depth-n grouplike at the shape parameter z_K \in F^\times.

By centrality of e_{\lambda_K} in H_{n_K}(q), the action of \beta \in B_{n_K} via the standard representation factors as

  \beta \cdot \alpha \cdot \beta^{-1}
  \;=\;
  (\beta \cdot e_{\lambda_K} \cdot \beta^{-1}) \cdot g(z_K)
  \;=\;
  e_{\lambda_K} \cdot g(z_K)
  \;=\; \alpha.

The braid-group action is trivial on \mathcal{H}_q^{(n, K)} — it fixes both factors (centrality + grouplike-as-scalar).

Step 2 (Galois action on the cell factorisation). The motivic- Galois action G_{\mathrm{mot}} acts on:

  • The coefficient ring F (cyclotomic Galois, bar involution etc.),
  • The shape parameter z_K \in F^\times.

It does not act on the partition \lambda_K directly, but through the bar involution it sends e_{\lambda_K} \to e_{\lambda_K'} (transpose partition). The factorisation transforms as:

  g_{\mathrm{mot}}(\alpha)
  \;=\;
  e_{\lambda_K'} \cdot g(g_{\mathrm{mot}}(z_K)).

Step 3 (joint composition). Compute the two composites:

  \begin{aligned}
    g_{\mathrm{mot}}(\beta \cdot \alpha)
    & \;=\; g_{\mathrm{mot}}(\alpha)
      \quad\text{(Step 1: braid trivial)} \\
    & \;=\; e_{\lambda_K'} \cdot g(g_{\mathrm{mot}}(z_K))
      \quad\text{(Step 2)} \\[4pt]
    \beta \cdot g_{\mathrm{mot}}(\alpha)
    & \;=\; \beta \cdot e_{\lambda_K'} \cdot g(g_{\mathrm{mot}}(z_K)) \cdot \beta^{-1} \\
    & \;=\; e_{\lambda_K'} \cdot g(g_{\mathrm{mot}}(z_K))
      \quad\text{(centrality of } e_{\lambda_K'}\text{).}
  \end{aligned}

Both expressions equal e_{\lambda_K'} \cdot g(g_{\mathrm{mot}}(z_K)). Joint commutativity holds. \square
